title: Evolution of Nonlinear Ion Transport in Nanopore Arrays: Ionic Conductance, Current Rectification, and Osmotic Power
abstract: Understanding the ionic transport and scaling behaviors in nanopore arrays is essential for bridging fundamental ion physics and blue energy applications. By fabricating sub-3 nm and sub-20 nm diameter nanopore arrays (NPAs) spanning from few pores to N ~ 10000, we systematically investigate ionic conductance, ion current rectification, and osmotic energy conversion. We report the ionic conductance scaling laws and nonlinearity with nanopore number, with stronger deviations from linearity at lower salt concentrations. Experimental evidence reveals that surface-charge-governed conductance and ion current rectification progressively weaken with increasing N and even vanish as the NPA scales up to N ~ 10000, resulting in an underestimation of surface charge density. In a sub-3 nm densely packed array (separation ~ 25 nm), the conductance exhibits an anomalous power-law dependence on concentration, deviating markedly from the single nanopore characteristics, attributed to the strong pore interactions. Furthermore, osmotic power harvesting measurements reveal a substantial reduction in power density upon scaling, with decreases of up to three orders of magnitude over the same range. To elucidate the underlying mechanism, we developed rigorous 3D modeling showing that the nonlinear behavior originates from concentration polarization at pore entrances and suppressed electric field across NPAs, collectively hindering ion transport. Our work provides insight into nonlinear ion-transport scaling and reveals fundamental differences between transport phenomena in single nanopores and nanopore arrays.
summary: This work systematically investigates how ionic conductance and energy harvesting scale in large nanopore arrays compared to single pores. The authors demonstrate that pore interactions, concentration polarization, and field suppression cause these properties to deviate significantly from simple linear scaling as the array size increases. This has major implications for designing nanoscale devices like desalination membranes.
main_problem: The study investigates how nonlinear ion transport phenomena, including ionic conductance, current rectification, and osmotic power generation, scale when moving from single nanopores to large arrays.
main_result: Conductance and current rectification effects significantly weaken or vanish as the number of pores increases, showing that simple scaling laws derived from single-pore models overestimate surface charge density. Osmotic power harvesting also shows a dramatic reduction upon upscaling to large arrays.
method: The research combines systematic experimental measurements on fabricated nanopore arrays with rigorous 3D numerical modeling based on Poisson-Nernst-Planck theory.
model_or_system: The physical system is solid-state nanopore arrays (NPAs) fabricated in $	ext{Si}_3	ext{N}_4$ membranes, studied across varying pore numbers ($N$) and diameters. The modeling involves solving the Poisson-Nernst-Planck equations to capture ion concentration polarization and electric field variations.
key_observables: Ionic conductance scaling laws ($	ext{G}_{	ext{NPA}}$ vs $N$), current rectification factor ($	ext{Rf}$), and osmotic power density.
important_parameters: Pore number ($N$ up to 10000), pore diameter (sub-3 nm to sub-20 nm), salt concentration, and interpore distance ($	ext{L}_{	ext{int}}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis often compares results against single nanopore models, which are shown to be insufficient for large arrays due to neglected pore interactions and polarization effects.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate fabrication methods (EBL/RIE vs. TEM-drilling), conductance measurements versus $N$ and concentration, $	ext{I-V}$ curves showing current rectification ($	ext{Rf}$ vs $N$), and power density scaling comparisons.
paper_structure: The paper systematically investigates the dependence of ionic transport properties on pore number ($N$) and salt concentration. It first establishes conductance scaling deviations from linearity, then analyzes current rectification weakening with $N$, and finally quantifies the dramatic reduction in osmotic power upon upscaling, attributing these effects to polarization and field suppression.
why_interesting: While focused on electrochemistry/materials science, the study of non-equilibrium transport phenomena (like ion flux under concentration gradients) involves complex many-body dynamics that share mathematical parallels with open quantum systems or strongly correlated charge transport models.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks
